Henry Luce. An American publisher and media mogul who founded Time magazine and later Life magazine, fundamentally shaping how twentieth-century Americans consumed news and visual information. Born to missionary parents in China, Luce pioneered the weekly news digest format and pioneered the large-format photojournalism magazine, making both publications primary cultural forces that shaped public opinion and visual literacy. His vision that Americans needed accessible, compelling storytelling about world events created a media empire that dominated American journalism for generations.

Luce founded Time magazine in nineteen-twenty-three with partner Briton Hadden, inventing the weekly news digest format to make world events digestible for busy readers. He pioneered the Man of the Year, now called Person of the Year, concept, which became a cultural touchstone for marking historical significance. In nineteen-thirty-six, he founded Life magazine as a large-format photojournalism publication, revolutionizing visual storytelling and making photography central to news media.

He built Time Incorporated into a massive publishing empire that also included Fortune and other influential magazines. Luce held deeply conservative political views and used his magazines as platforms for his anti-communist ideology during the Cold War. He championed what he called the American Century, the idea that American cultural and political dominance was inevitable and desirable in the postwar world.

He employed renowned photographers like Margaret Bourke-White, whose stunning work helped define the visual aesthetic of twentieth-century journalism.
